en: The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-arthavyākhyā*, Scroll Four.
It is explained that this is mentioned later because it was heard [later]. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is precisely within this section that it is clarified;
this is also the sequential order. ... [He] is able to manifest in the form of a woman, and is also able to practice...
It is not the Way;
it is by means of this that one penetrates the Right Way.
The Buddha is the fruit of ultimate perfection.
Because those who practice the Way together with [the Buddhas] are able to attain penetration,
and because people reach the state of Buddhahood through this, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Buddha-Way" (*Fódǎo pǐn*).
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.

By practicing on the non-path, he brings to an end the distinction between the jewel-like and the ordinary; though the Buddha’s path may appear remote, it thereby reveals that the Bodhisattva possesses the virtue of embracing all beings.
This eclipses the way of solitary self-cultivation characteristic of the Two Vehicles.
Within this chapter, it is divided into two distinct sections.
From the beginning of the chapter until the point where it says "forever unable to give rise to the mind for the Unsurpassed Way," it correctly elucidates the meaning of penetrating the Buddha-way.
From the passage beginning with "Thereafter, from Universal Manifestation of the Body" (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*) onwards, this is a question posed by Ākāśagarbha;
however, no separate chapter title is established for it,
as it is elucidated by being appended here.
Within the context of the Buddha-way, this is divided into three sections.
The first begins from the start of the chapter and concludes with the passage, "A bodhisattva can thus practice on what is not the Way," which constitutes the thorough penetration of the Buddha-way.
This directly clarifies the meaning of the non-existence of practice.

Second, from Vimalakīrti’s question to Mañjuśrī regarding what constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata, up to the point that "if one does not enter the great ocean of afflictions, one cannot obtain the jewel of omniscience."

This clarifies that, speaking in terms of conditions, it is because the Buddha’s [teaching]—the seal of the afflictions of birth and death—is the seed of the Tathāgata that one is able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

Third, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Mahākāśyapa sighed" onwards, Kāśyapa praises and recounts the words of Mañjuśrī while simultaneously expressing his own lamentation regarding his present state.
Regarding the first section on penetrating the Buddha-way,
Vimalakīrti stated that "a bodhisattva practicing non-ways is what constitutes penetrating the Buddha-way.
Now, [the text] speaks of these as "non-ways."
Except for the true path of the Bodhisattva, all else is considered a non-path.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s merit lies in harmonizing with light by appearing as one with it;
that is, while traversing what is not the path, the inner mind remains untainted, thereby embodying the Way.
Rightly, one penetrates the Buddha-way;
it is by means of the provisional practices that the Way is not bypassed,
and only then does the true Way attain penetration.
The practices of both things and the self are fully realized.
Therefore, it is said that practicing what is not the Way is itself the thorough penetration of the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, he asked: "What is it to practice within what is not the Way?"
If a bodhisattva were to be identical with the defilements, they would necessarily be subject to defilement.
How then can they be identical with what is non-existent and yet remain free from evil?
The answer is as follows:
Regarding one who commits the five acts of immediate retribution yet remains free from affliction and anger:
evil arises from the mind and does not reside in external phenomena or principles;
thus, it is shown that although they commit the five heinous crimes, their inner mind is without hatred.
Therefore, their evils are not the same.
Within this, it is divided into four sections.
The first section covers the five acts of immediate retribution up to the hungry ghosts, wherein meritorious qualities are fully present.
To practice unwholesome paths due to evil causes and the fruits of evil virtues— specifically,
to commit the five acts of immediate retribution without feeling affliction or anger—
is the most grievous cause among evils.
Ordinary people mostly commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) out of an intense mind of affliction and anger.
It is impossible for one who desires [to act] to actually carry out the five heinous crimes without affliction and anger.
The hells, animals, and hungry ghosts are precisely the fruits of these [crimes].
Generally, those who fall into hell do so because of their sinful defilements;
although the Great Being appears to dwell therein, he is in fact free from sinful defilements.
Because [beings] abound in such [faults], they fall among the animals.
This is intended to clarify that although Bodhisattvas manifest in animal forms, their ignorance and pride have long since been severed.
Because they are stingy, greedy, and of meager merit, lacking all virtues, they fall among the hungry ghosts.
Although the Great Being dwells within it, his merit is already complete.
This is the second sub-section,
which cites the path of the Form Realm.
Regarding "not considering [them] superior":
this clarifies that one practices non-pathways based on wholesome causes and wholesome fruits;
the realms of form and formlessness are precisely what constitute wholesome fruits.
The Way is a virtuous cause.
This is intended to clarify that although a Great Being manifests within it, he cannot be surpassed by it.
This is the third sub-section.
Having demonstrated the practice of desire and having demonstrated the practice of all afflictions, his mind remains ever pure.
Generally speaking, he understands that all afflictions arise from causes and proceed through what is not the Path;
thus, while demonstrating the practice of desire, he remains free from all defiled attachments.
This clarifies that although a bodhisattva manifests conduct identical to that of desire, they are free from the fault of defiled attachment.
The subsequent phrases may be understood by analogy with this.
Thus, it is said: "Though manifesting the practice of all afflictions, the mind remains ever pure."
This collectively enumerates all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the causes of affliction cannot be fully described, they are summarized and bound together as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
This is intended to clarify that while the Bodhisattva’s afflictions exist externally, his mind is pure within and free from attachment.
The fourth sub-section.
From "showing entry into Māra" onwards, it concludes with the non-interruption of birth and death;
herein, it clarifies that one practices non-ways by means of various karmic retributions.
Regarding the statement, "Manifesting entry into Māra while following the Buddha’s wisdom and not following the teachings of others":
this is intended to clarify that while a bodhisattva outwardly appears identical to the various māras, inwardly they accord with right wisdom and do not follow the teachings of Māra.
The subsequent categories may be understood accordingly.
As for manifesting entry into all paths,
the retributive fruits thereof cannot be fully described.
This concludes the summary by way of the resultant retribution.
Nirvāṇa is presented separately because it lies outside the scope of resultant retribution.
The passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva was able to do this" concludes the meaning of practicing on non-paths to attain penetration of the Buddha-path.
From the point where Vimalakīrti questions Mañjuśrī onwards constitutes the second major section.
The seeds are explained in terms of their conditions.
The reason for questioning Mañjuśrī is to clarify that these two sages mutually illuminate one another.
Within this, it is divided into three sections.
The first begins from "At that time, Vimalakīrti... and concludes with "...all afflictions are the seeds of the Buddha.
This clarifies that the term "seeds" is explained in reference to various evils.
As for why afflictions constitute the seed of the Tathāgata:
if one discusses this according to principle,
the myriad practices are the seeds of Buddhahood.
Now, afflictions are designated as the seeds.
If there were no afflictions, one would be unable to resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment].
It is by taking afflictions as a condition that one generates the bodhicitta.
This refers to the "seeds" (bīja) mentioned within this context.
Furthermore, it is explained that afflictions (kleśa) are designated as seeds for this reason.
Now it is explained that the arising of the Dharma is not fixed; it issues forth from conditions,
such that one may turn away from the heterodox toward the orthodox,
or reform evil to cultivate goodness.
This is precisely because the right arises from the wrong,
and the good is produced from the evil; therefore,
conditions are able to differentiate the seeds.
The preceding clarified the merit of the teacher who takes what is not the Way as the Way;
now this clarifies the virtue of the disciple who takes what is not a seed-lineage as the seed-lineage.
This shows that the Two Vehicles, being solely concerned with their own self-benefit, lack the merit of the teacher.
One who lacks the seeds of affliction loses the virtue of a disciple.
As for "possessing a body," the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root of all precepts.
From "ignorance" and "desire-attachment" onwards, the meaning of the "incremental one" (*eka-vṛddhi*) is explained in detail with respect to the various afflictions.

Regarding the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*): the humans and devas of the desire realm constitute one; the three dhyānas and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) constitute the [remaining] seven.
The reason one does not take rebirth in the three miserable realms is simply that these three realms are places of intense suffering,
where consciousness finds no pleasure in dwelling.
Therefore, it is not taken up.
The fourth dhyāna consists only of the mind of the fourth dhyāna;
the state of non-perception (asaṃjñi) is the meditative absorption of the cessation of the mind (nirodhasamāpatti).
Consciousness does not delight in dwelling [there],
and for that reason it is not grasped.
As for "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," it refers simply to the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as maintained within the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Therefore, consciousness does not delight in dwelling [there].
This concludes the second sub-section.
It says: "What is meant by this? and so forth, ending with: "Therefore, one should know that all afflictions are the seeds of the Tathāgata."
This clarifies the resolution of doubts.
What is meant by this? It refers to words that give rise to doubt:
[one might wonder] that the ultimate, wondrous fruit should depend upon a superior cause to serve as its seed.
Now, as for the statement that "afflictions serve as seeds," what is its intended meaning?
The answer is:
if one perceives the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), this refers to the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā).
Regarding those who enter the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) yet are unable to arouse the bodhicitta:
the "stage of correctness" refers here to that which cannot lead one upward.

This clarifies that persons of the Two Vehicles are weary of worldly toil; their minds dwell in the principle of quiescence and fear, finding self-comfort in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus severing their resolve for that which lies beyond the mundane world.
Since the afflictions of ordinary beings are heavy, the suffering they encounter is even heavier;

yet, upon hearing the teaching of ultimate bliss, they are able to give rise to a resolve for the realm beyond the mundane. This constitutes the stage of "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind" (Cittotpāda-vihāra).
If we speak according to principle,
those of the two vehicles were both already destined to attain Buddhahood first; however,
the reason for making this statement now is as follows.
This is to cause those of the Two Vehicles to appreciate the beauty of polishing and refining, so that ordinary beings may give rise to the aspiration for the supreme [Buddha-vehicle].
It is like a high plateau where lotus flowers do not grow;
there are three similes following this.
The first two analogies apply generally to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
while the latter one applies specifically to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*).
The fact that lotuses do not grow on high plateaus serves as a metaphor for the Two Vehicles.
The phrase "low-lying, damp mud" is a metaphor for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Likewise, the passage beginning with "having thus seen the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)" corresponds to the aforementioned "high ground and dry land.
The passage beginning with "within the mud of afflictions (*kleśa*)" corresponds to the aforementioned "low-lying, damp mud."
Furthermore, the subsequent passage regarding "planting seeds in the air" also provides analogies for both ordinary persons and noble ones; however,
the former was spoken with reference to the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mūḍha-anuśaya*),
whereas this is stated in terms of the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*).
Therefore, they may be considered distinct.
Furthermore, planting seeds in the air serves as a metaphor for the followers of the Two Vehicles,
while fertile soil that has been composted serves as a metaphor for ordinary beings.
Those who perceive the unconditioned plant seeds in the void;
those who give rise to the view of self on ground that is utterly ruined by excrement give rise to a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru.
This clarifies that because ordinary beings harbor a sense of self and are naturally arrogant, they follow only what they deem superior;
thus, upon hearing of the Buddha’s fruit of ultimate bliss, they look up to it with admiration and yearning.
Therefore, one should know that the following section summarizes how all [beings] are of the Tathāgata lineage.
The third sub-section uses analogies, such as that of not descending [from a mountain], specifically to illustrate the Two Vehicles.
The first two analogies clarify that the Two Vehicles lack the virtue of disciples,
while the final analogy clarifies their lack of the merit of a teacher.
In general, those who wish to obtain the jewel must personally traverse the great ocean.

Śrāvakas do not enter [the realm of] birth and death... [omitted] ...whereas Bodhisattvas enter birth and death and thereby attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that they obtain the jewel of unsurpassed wisdom.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa exclaimed, "Excellent! This marks the third major section.
From "Excellent" onwards, the text clarifies the praise and narration of Mañjuśrī’s words:
those who are companions in the afflictions are truly able to resolve their minds for the sake of the seed of Buddhahood.

"We are now no longer capable" and the following passage clarifies that the followers of the Two Vehicles lament their own lack of capacity and cannot resolve to awaken, while praising the ability of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) to do so.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, ordinary worldlings possess a sense of reciprocity toward the Buddha-dharma, whereas the Śrāvakas do not.
Ordinary beings show gratitude toward the Buddha's Dharma;
for the Buddha’s original intention was solely to have compassion for those in suffering.
Thus, ordinary beings are able to give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Extensively transforming sentient beings accords with the Buddha’s original intention;
since the duty of repaying his kindness is fulfilled,
it is said that there is reciprocity.
Furthermore, the śrāvakas also receive the teachings and practice them;
however, they merely sever the afflictions of the three realms and fully realize nirvana,
being unable to perform transformative teachings for sentient beings.
This deviates from the Buddha’s intention;
therefore, it is said that there is no sense of returning or reciprocation.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
Do not [distinguish] between ordinary people and sages; since beginningless time, all have once generated the great resolve, though they forgot it in the interim.
Now, these ordinary people again generate the great resolve.
This accords with the original ancient interpretation;
hence it is said that [the two vehicles] turn back.
Persons of the two vehicles are utterly devoid of the capacity for the Mahāyāna.
Because one does not return to one's original practice, it is said that there is no returning. Why is this so?
The following explains the meaning of the presence or absence [of such returning] for both ordinary persons and sages.
Why is it that ordinary persons possess the quality of returning, whereas śrāvakas do not?
The explanation states:
when ordinary persons hear the Buddha-dharma, they are able to give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
They resolve their minds to attain Buddhahood;
the transmission of the teaching remains unbroken,
and those who achieve awakening continue in succession.
The Three Jewels are never interrupted;
because there is the principle of repaying kindness,
there is reciprocity.
Even if a śrāvaka were to hear the Buddha-dharma,
they would ultimately be unable to give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed path;
therefore, there is no returning.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samantavabhāsarūpakāya... [as follows, ending with] the Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality.
This concludes the fourth treatise on Subhūti’s Emptiness.
Because the house was empty, Puxian asked:
"Ordinary people’s households should have parents, wives, children, and kinsmen, as well as the means of livelihood for taking and giving.
Layman, where are these things?"
Vimalakīrti replied, "Great Mahāsattva, you differ from the people of the world.
Worldly people take birth and death as their parents, wives, children, and kinsmen;
they take conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as their means of livelihood."
The two wisdoms of the Great Being—expedient means and reality—are his parents;
his merits serve as his wife, children, retinue, and the necessities of life.
Although he knows there is neither arising nor ceasing, he clarifies expedient means, extensively elaborating upon the meaning of the father.
The Chapter on the Non-dual Dharma Gate extensively explains the meaning of the Mother [Prajñāpāramitā].
Subsequently, five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
all of them had come from the empty room.

The Universal Manifestation of Physical Bodies (Samantavyūha-rūpakāya) has long since emerged from the empty chamber; now, through this initial section, it is shown that while the provisional realms do not encompass all that is non-path or unwholesome, the Buddha’s true path is revealed here as being complete with every virtue.
Because virtue is complete within, one is able to harmonize externally with what is not the Way and approach it.
This section is divided into four parts.
The first, from the beginning, explains where all these things are located.
The first part clarifies that because the chamber is empty, the Universal Manifestation Body (Prabhūtarūpakāya) arises; this constitutes the question.

The second part begins from "Thereupon, Vimalakīrti replied with a verse" and continues until the section on "subduing the four kinds of Māras and erecting the banner of victory at the site of enlightenment."
The clarity of the parents' kinsmen and their means of livelihood differs from that of the world.
Third, although one knows there is no arising or ceasing, for the sake of manifesting it to others, there is birth.
[This continues] from here until the end of the chapter.
The "Chapter on the Wisdom of Skillful Means" elucidates the meaning of the father, which is broad;
the fourth chapter, "Entering the Dharma-Door of Non-Duality," elucidates the meaning of the mother, which is real wisdom.
As for why the first section, "The Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body," poses a question:
Now, within a dwelling there ought to be parents, kinsmen, and the various articles for livelihood;
yet none of these are present here.
For this reason, he asks:
"Where are my parents, wife, and children?
Where are all the elephants, horses, and carriages?
Vimalakīrti then answered him with a verse, which is divided into three sections.
From the first [chapter], "The Perfection of Wisdom" (*Prajñāpāramitā*), down to this point, it constitutes the musical performance.
There are four verses in *gāthā* meter,
spoken with reference to the person's retinue.
Regarding the statement that "the Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Bodhisattvas and skillful means is the father":
the mother is fundamentally the one who manages the household affairs within the inner chambers;
because the desire to clarify actual wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) relies upon the internal principle, it is taken as the mother.
The father was originally intended to be a guest of honor;
he rectified affairs in foreign lands,
and thus his external transformation was like that of a father.
There are no teachers of any path who do not arise from these;
these two types of wisdom nourish the Dharma-body and are the root of the myriad practices.
How could they be merely the parents of Bodhisattvas?
All Buddhas are likewise born from this.
Regarding "taking the joy of the Dharma as one's wife":
a wife is fundamentally that to which one's will is wedded.
Because the joy of the Dharma is so refreshing and pleasant, it is taken as one's wife.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
when people of the world take a wife, they do so to seek offspring to carry on the family lineage.
It is like a path arising from joy;
because of that joy, the lineage of the Buddha continues and the Dharma-body remains unbroken,
just as a family line is sustained through the taking of a wife and children so that the progeny does not cease.
Regarding "taking the mind of compassion as a daughter":
a woman has the quality of going outward;
because compassion extends outwardly, it is said to be a daughter.
Another interpretation:
Women’s nature is characterized by abundant compassion;
because he harbors a mind of compassion that resembles the nature of women, he uses them as a metaphor.
A man of virtuous mind and sincerity is one whose masculine integrity and capability enable him to manage household affairs; this is the meaning.
To clarify that the goodness of sincerity possesses the utility of integrity and capability, such that he can manage the household affairs of the Buddha-fruit Bodhi.
Regarding the "ultimately empty and quiescent dwelling":
"dwelling" (she) signifies a place where the body finds rest;
"emptiness" (kong) is the abode where the spirit resides.
It is like a house;
another interpretation is that a house fundamentally serves to ward off wind and frost and to shield against rain and dew.
This realization of the principle of emptiness can obstruct the winds and frosts of afflictions and shield against the rain and dew of the outflows (*āsrava*).
As for the statement, "The disciples' various defilements are turned according to the will [of the mind]," the fundamental meaning of a disciple is to receive and uphold the teacher's instructions.
This clarifies that sentient beings amidst the afflictions who receive transformation from me possess the meaning of being my disciples.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
a disciple is one who respects and obeys, provides filial support and nourishment, and benefits me.
Because the merit from enlightening sentient beings who are immersed in worldly toil comes back to benefit oneself, one is said to have disciples.
Those who attain perfect enlightenment through the factors of the path and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are such that these spiritual friends are able to benefit them by means of virtuous signs.
It is precisely because the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) provide the necessary support for attaining Buddhahood that they are called "knowledge" (jñāna).
Regarding the "companions in the dharmas of the various perfections" (pāramitā):
when people of the world travel across rivers or over mountain passes, they must form groups and rely on steadfast companions before they can proceed.
To clarify that if a Mahāsattva wishes to traverse the rivers and streams of birth and death and cross the frontier passes of affliction,
there is no way to proceed without being accompanied by the six perfections; therefore,
they are described as his "equal companions."
Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) as female entertainers:
they are called female entertainers because the four means of integration accord with sentient beings and delight their sentiments.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
Performers originally take sound as their purpose;
they will surely attract many people,
and by employing the four means of integration to transform sentient beings, they will accord with the inclinations of those beings.
The multitude will surely follow and submit to it.
Those who chant and recite the words of the Dharma as their music do so because the music of worldly people is used merely for self-comfort and gratification.
The Bodhisattva finds delight in the sound of the Dharma.
The second section, beginning with "The Garden of Total Retention" and ending with "Purifying the Mind as Bathing and the Precepts as Ointment," [describes this].
The seven verses clarify that there are differences in the means of sustenance.
Regarding "the garden of dhāraṇī":
a garden is fundamentally protected by a fence so that its fruits are not lost.
This is intended to clarify that the dhāraṇī’s total retention of the characteristics of sounds is not lost.
Regarding the forest trees of the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas:
because the roots of the trees of the untainted state attained through the vision of the truths are deep and difficult to uproot, their branches and foliage flourish luxuriantly.
The tongue is like a tree because it manifests the outflows-free (anāsrava), profound, firm, and unshakable [wisdom], with the branches of myriad virtues flourishing and spreading.
Furthermore, just as a single body of tree can shield the sunlight, it possesses the significance of providing cool shade.
This clarifies that the essence of this outflow-free state can obstruct the sunlight of false views and afflictions, thereby attaining the cool and wondrous bliss of nirvana.
"The pure and exquisite flower of awakened mind and the fruit of the wisdom of liberation" refers to this.
Just as flowers originally arise from trees and can produce fruit,

so too does the tree of the untainted vision of the truths give rise to the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment through contemplation, thereby attaining the fruit of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, which is liberation.
Regarding "the bathing pool of the eight liberations, filled with the limpid waters of meditative concentration":
the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the stages of transcendence (*abhibhvāyatana*) eliminate the lower evil realms,
just as a bathing pool removes impurities.
Now, one who wishes to cultivate the practice of the eight liberations must cause the mind to roam within the waters of meditative concentration.
If the cultivation of concentration is perfected,
then the pool of the eight liberations will be filled.
Therefore, it is said that "the water of concentration is filled to the brim.
As for the phrase "arrayed with the flowers of the seven purities, these are people free from defilement," these seven purities are:

purity of precepts, purity of mind, purity of view, purity through overcoming doubt, purity regarding what is and is not the path, purity of practice, and purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of practice.
This is called the Seven Purities (*saptaviśuddhi*).
"Flower" (*puṣpa*) fundamentally carries the meaning of being fragrant and fresh-pure.
This clarifies that when the seven purities—precepts, concentration, fragrance, and wisdom—are complete, they are fresh and pure, just like a flower.
The Arhats and Dharmakāya Mahāsattvas roam their minds within this principle;
therefore it is said, "He bathes these stainless persons.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Just as flowers originally emerge from water and are thus able to adorn trees,
so too these seven purifications arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and thereby adorn the elephant-like concentration that gallops with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The Bodhisattva, by means of the five supernormal powers, flies and travels everywhere to transform sentient beings,
just as an elephant or horse gallops at full speed.
The Mahāyāna is taken as the chariot.
The Mahāyāna has the meaning of "carrying across," for it is like a vehicle.
One who is guided by a single mind travels upon the Eightfold Path.
Although the Eightfold Noble Path is indeed level and smooth,
if there were no Great Vehicle chariot to guide and control it, there would be the danger of straying from its course.
"Single-mindedness" refers to the mind of relinquishment.
The mind has three characteristics:
first, activation;
second, withdrawal.
Third is the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
If the mind is overly agitated, one should cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
if the mind is overly sunken, one should cultivate diligence (*vīrya*).
If movement and stillness are harmoniously adjusted,
allowing them to proceed naturally within a state of composure and ease,
this is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
When one practices equanimity, it is like a skilled charioteer:
if the oxen lag, he prods them;
if they are too fast, he restrains them.
When the pace is appropriately regulated,
one may proceed gradually along the level path without encountering any obstacles or difficulties.
To be fully endowed with a majestic countenance and adorned with the various marks of excellence is to embellish one’s physical form.
His countenance is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man,
and his features are embellished by the eighty minor characteristics.
These are the supreme garments of shame and modesty.
In the world, superior clothing takes its meaning from concealing what is worn-out and tattered.

It is intended to clarify that for a bodhisattva, the self-possessed qualities of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) constitute superior clothing, established to manifest the concealment of the black, tattered, and base states of shamelessness and lack of dread of blame.
Regarding "the profound mind as a flower garland":
in the world, a flower garland is an ornament for the head;
this is intended to clarify that the practice of the profound mind is superior, just like a garland.
Furthermore,
it is explained that just as worldly people string together various flowers with a thread to fashion them into a head ornament,

this illustrates how a Bodhisattva uses the understanding of their profound resolve to string together all practices based on the fundamental principle, ultimately achieving the adornment of the head of wisdom.
One who possesses the seven treasures of wealth consists of faith,
precepts, learning, wisdom, generosity, shame, and remorse— these are called the seven treasures.
In the world, people consider abundance in the seven precious gems to be wealth.
The Great Being accumulates these seven dharmas as his wealth.
To cause them to flourish through instruction means to teach and transform others by means of the seven riches.
If people further transform others,
and these transformations are passed on in succession, how could they not increase and proliferate?
As it has been said, practicing and dedicating the merit constitutes a great benefit.
As it is said, one should practice accordingly;
dedicating the roots of goodness cultivated toward the attainment of the unsurpassed path,
one allows the merit to accrue to oneself.
It is like a great benefit.
Regarding the statement that the four dhyānas serve as a bed and seat arising from pure livelihood:
a bed and seat provide a place for reclining and resting to settle the body.
The fourth dhyāna signifies tranquility, which is equivalent to sitting upon a couch.
Furthermore,
it is explained that couches and seats in the world are used to avoid venomous stings and dampness.

Among causes, that which brings about the fruit of suffering is called "sin," while that which induces happiness is called "merit.

Suffering and its origin are with outflows;

This void and existence are relative and thus constitute duality.
If one is free from all numerical designations, then the mind is like space.

even seeking space, it cannot be found.

from the signless state upward, upon attaining true outflow-free wisdom, it is termed the supramundane mind.

Within the principle of emptiness, one does not perceive the mundane mind entering into birth and death, nor the supramundane mind emerging from birth and death; furthermore, one does not perceive the mundane mind overflowing within birth and death, nor the supramundane mind dispersing and extinguishing within birth and death.

for within the principle of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), both exhaustion and non-exhaustion are empty and unobtainable, and thus one does not speak of exhaustion. Pushou said: "I" and "no-self" [are likewise].

Within the principle of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), even a divine self (*puruṣa*) does not exist;

The Deva Dian said: "Luminosity and non-luminosity constitute duality.
Wisdom is luminosity;
afflictions are non-luminosity."
"The true nature of ignorance is itself illumination" means that because the essence of the true nature of ignorance is empty, it is itself illumination.
"Illumination, too, cannot be grasped and is beyond all numerical categories."

"The Buddha has taught the eight liberations;

The Buddha has taught the eight liberations.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that although there were eight liberations in the past,

This is merely a statement made from the perspective of the most prominent conditions;

This may also be understood through the perspective of multiple treatises.

The third [section], from "Because the minds of those difficult to transform are like monkeys" down to "Only through harsh and urgent words can they be brought into the practice of the precepts."

The first sub-section, beginning with "The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform," concludes by clearly citing two analogies to show that such matters require words of firm strength.

first, one is frequently subjected to slander;

Harsh speech has two fruits:

Idle speech has two fruits:

second, one is unable to express oneself with clarity and precision.
Greed has two fruits:
first, excessive desire;
second, lack of contentment.
Hatred has two fruits:
first, one constantly seeks out the faults and shortcomings of others;

The third banner:
this is stinginess, this is the retribution for stinginess, and this is delusion.

Those who violate the precepts...

it employs two parables to conclude that the matter requires words of firm severity.
The restless agitation of monkeys is a metaphor for the myriad activities of the mind;
the unruliness of elephants and horses is a metaphor for the rigidity and strength of the physical form and speech of body and mouth.
When that bodhisattva has heard this being explained, [this concludes] the sixth major section within the middle fascicle.
The Great Beings from the upper realms marveled at both the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, exclaiming, "This is truly unprecedented!

being humble, they do not shrink from toil nor do they discriminate between the pure and the impure.
Born in this land.
From the words "following the speech of Vimalakīrti" onwards is the seventh major section,
which describes and confirms his words.
He sighed, "The great compassion and firm resolve of the bodhisattvas in this land are truly as you have described.

However, from the passage beginning with "Yet, in a single lifetime" onwards, it clarifies that practice in the defiled land is superior to that in the pure land.
Nevertheless, wisdom arises by depending on ignorance, and goodness is elicited by means of evil.
Because evil is abundant, the goodness it elicits is profound;
because folly is prevalent, the wisdom it gives rise to is substantial.
All of these rely upon external conditions as powerful catalysts;
only then can the firm resolve of internal understanding be awakened.
Therefore, it is said that practicing for a single lifetime in this world surpasses eons of practice in the Pure Land.
Why is this? It is because the following explains the sense in which practicing in a defiled land is superior to a pure land.
As for why practicing in a defiled land is superior to a pure land, it clarifies that there are briefly ten kinds of wholesome dharmas in the defiled land of Sahā.
This is absent in the Pure Land.
By means of giving, one gathers in those who are poor;
this constitutes the essence of the ten matters.
Because the defiled land possesses poverty, one is able to fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
In the pure land, there is no poverty or strife;
since this practice is lacking there, it is shown that the defiled land is superior to the pure land.
It is like a skilled physician who, during an eon of simulated illness,
masters medical arts and dispenses excellent medicine to the sick so that all their desires for healing are fulfilled.
It is likewise with the Bodhisattva who dwells in impure lands to transform sentient beings.
As their various practices flourish, they attain the ten expansive dharmas and become great medicinal kings to deliver all sentient beings; thus,
they are able to transcend ten thousand kalpas and eliminate the maladies of affliction and birth-and-death.
These words are all intended for those at the beginning of their practice in this defiled land, so as to cause them to exhaust their own resolve.
The passage beginning with "That bodhisattva said: 'In how many dharmas is a bodhisattva accomplished? constitutes the eighth major section.
The Great Being of the Upper Direction clarifies the practice of the Pure Land for those newly raised in this land;
he clarifies that those who have only begun the practice, whose meritorious deeds are not yet perfected, are unable to extricate themselves.
It is like a weak person who enters the water to rescue someone drowning; unable to accomplish both tasks, he perishes along with the other.
It was for the sake of causing the newly initiated bodhisattvas of this land to cultivate the practices for purifying a buddha-field that he posed this question.
Another interpretation is as follows:

When those at the beginning of their practice heard the aforementioned statement—that benefiting sentient beings in this world for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas exceeds [the merit of] practicing in that land—they concluded that the Bodhisattva’s compassion lies in the defiled lands and that one who does not cultivate pure practices will remain stuck in the defiled realm. Therefore, they requested the practice of the Pure Land to advance their own spiritual progress.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the practice of purifying the buddha-field.
Those who give rise to birth in a pure land through practice free from blemishes possess virtuous conduct as fresh and pure as a thoroughly cleansed body.
To record evil while harboring goodness is like having sores and tumors.
Regarding these eight dharmas, the meaning is clarified in four sections.
In the first section, the relationship between honoring those above and assisting those below is presented.
Benefiting sentient beings without expecting recompense, being ultimately humble and unimpeded—
this clarifies the first phrase of the following line:
regarding all bodhisattvas as one regards a Buddha.

rather, one should subdue the mind therein.
This concludes the section on the meaning of correctly maintaining the superior attainment and loss.
In the fourth section, one contrasts oneself with others and constantly reflects upon one's own faults.
In the seventh [section], one reflects inwardly within oneself regarding one's own transgressions.
The eighth phrase means not to litigate when seeing the faults of others,
but to always seek all merits with a single mind,
thereby fulfilling the aforementioned meaning of benefiting both self and others.
This concludes the ninth major section of the Mañjuśrī-parivarta, which clarifies how the preaching of the Dharma benefits all people and leads them to the realization of the Way.
As for the arrival of this chapter, it is the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice" (Bodhisattvacaryā-parivarta). This is the reason why this chapter has come forth.
Bodhisattvas from the upper realms, who are at the beginning of their practice, may conceive inferior notions regarding this land;
the Tathāgata has extensively clarified that while the Buddha-activities of the worlds of the ten directions differ, the merits of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are equal.
It is said that when the Bodhisattvas and Mahāsattvas of the Upper Direction, including Ānanda, came to personally seek repentance, request the Dharma, and return to their own land,

Within this chapter, there are eight sections that clarify the meaning.

In the upper direction, the bodhisattvas offered various kinds of incense and flowers as an act of worship to express their feelings of jubilation.

At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "The fragrance we have now smelled is unlike anything experienced since antiquity.
This is the third section,
which extensively clarifies the distinctions in the benefits of the fragrant food by means of a question regarding its scent.
The question regarding the fragrance from the pores of that bodhisattva is intended to cause Śāriputra to speak and answer for himself. As for the question,
"How long will such a fragrance persist?"— it is meant to elicit his own response.
Question: How long does the fragrance remain?
Answer: The potency of this food lasts for seven days;
it is not necessarily limited to seven days.
However, the people of Jambudvīpa can survive on nothing but this for only seven days;
thus, it is said to be "seven days" because the statement is made with reference to a single region.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
It is the natural law that those who have not yet entered the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) for seven days are persons of the stage of the Śrāvaka lineage;
those who have entered the state of certainty are at the level of the signless (*animitta*) and above;
and those who have attained right liberation have realized the fourth fruit.
Ordinary persons who have not yet generated the mind of the Mahāyāna;
those who have already generated that intention but abide in the stages prior to the [first] ground;
and those who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) up to and including the seventh ground.
Furthermore, regarding the first stage:
those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood are Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
Although this fragrant rice is a condition for attaining the Way on lower stages, [it is not so for those at the highest level].
If one asks whether those from the first bhūmi upward rely on this to enter the Path,
it is said "up to the tenth bhūmi" because one desires to establish that the benefit of the fragrant rice has both a beginning and an end.
Likewise, in the Hīnayāna, one should also speak of the first, second, and third fruits, up to the fourth fruit.
It is merely that the text is abbreviated.
Within the section on the Bodhisattvas, there should likewise be a progression from the first and second stages up to the single stage;
however, it is omitted in the text.
This extensively clarifies that the Buddha-activities throughout the worlds of the ten directions differ, and the entryways into the Way are manifold:
there are those who attain the Way through the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*),
and there are also those who receive benefit through the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
This method is realized through the auditory consciousness.
As for the phrase "extinguishing all poisons of the afflictions," it refers to the partial severance of the specific portions belonging to that particular stage.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha with the following fourth section,
clarifying that the Buddha’s activities differ [from those of others] and proving that the fragrant rice possesses actual benefit.
Regarding how the Buddha performs buddha-work through his radiance:
Since one obtains the subtle [realization] through the light of insight,
these [phenomena] assist in performing the Buddha-work.
Furthermore, it is by means of bodhisattvas that the Buddha-work is performed.
Just as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, after entering such meditative absorption, delivered six million billion *gaṅgā*-sands of people by means of the sixteen prince-bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, as for the person emanated by the Buddha:
after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Suśānta, he left behind a single transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to remain in the world and preach the Dharma.
As for the Bodhisattva tree: [it is so called because]...
His light shines everywhere without exception;
his fragrance permeates all without fail;
and his physical form is subtle and wondrous, appearing according to the inclinations of those who behold it.
It emits wondrous sounds that are heard according to the inclinations of each being;
those among sentient beings who transgress do not fail to enter the Path.
Furthermore, as for the Buddha’s robes:

Just as when the King of Jambudvīpa, during a time of worldly pestilence, invited the Buddha and received the *saṃghāṭī* robe from the Buddha and the Saṃgha; by prostrating to it, he gave rise to wholesome roots,
his illness was cured, and furthermore,
he provided them with food and drink.
The fragrant pavilions and gardens are all made of fragrance.
As for the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics,
each mark manifests in accordance with what is appropriate to lead sentient beings into the Way.
Regarding the Buddha-body:

it refers to the wondrous substance of the manifested form (*nirmāṇakāya*). There is a distinction because the former discusses the specific marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), while the latter speaks of the Buddha-body in general.
Regarding space: [it is]...
In the midst of the clamor, he manifested empty space.
Furthermore,
it is explained that Mañjuśrī extinguished all forms and appearances in order to transform King Ajātaśatru.
Regarding those sentient beings who should be guided by these conditions:
they should enter into correct practice by means of the causes and conditions explained above.
As for "dreams and illusions":
These six similes are taught to enable people to attain awakening.
Furthermore, it is explained that they manifest according to what should be seen by each individual.
It is like seeing a rākṣasa in a dream.
If that is so, why is it called a "simile"?
It is simply because these six are frequently used as similes throughout the sūtras.
In the preaching of the Dharma through sounds and speech, these many [beings] take vocal instruction as their Buddha-work.
In the pure Buddha-lands, there is silence and no speech; this is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Just as the Tathāgata Dharmatā has clarified, the Bodhisattvas from the lower direction do not delight in dwelling among the multitude or in various discourses; they perform Buddha-work by being tranquil, compliant, and unconditioned.

The pure Buddha-fields are brilliantly manifest in the realm of the insentient; they come from nowhere, are beyond speech, and are tranquil, unconditioned, and spontaneous in their advancement toward the Way.
Thus, Ānanda, such are the majestic deportment, the movements, and all the actions performed by the Buddhas.
It clarifies that every movement of the Great Sage possesses benefit;
therefore, there is nothing that is not a Buddha-activity.
These four māras and various afflictions are merely gateways [to it].
When sentient beings become exhausted by this, the Buddhas perform buddha-work through this very method:
they are mostly able to subdue venomous dragons whose power and extreme anger have been stilled, first binding them with desire and subsequently instructing people with the Dharma.
All such examples are Buddha-activities;
it is precisely through these teachings that one is led to enter the Way.
This is called "entering the dharma-gate of all Buddhas."
To summarize the above, these ritual procedures for Buddha-activities and daily practices constitute the essential nature of the Dharma.
Regarding "the Bodhisattva who enters this gate," the following is the fifth section.
The text clearly states that Ānanda addressed the Bodhisattva Fangshang:
"If a bodhisattva enters this gate, their performance of Buddha-works will differ from others.
If they see all pure and excellent buddha-fields and do not feel joy, nor harbor greed or pride, [they enter this gate]."
Since the Buddha's activities differ,
even when one sees what is pure and beautiful, no joy arises and there is no attachment, nor does one regard it as superior;
likewise, if one sees what is impure, one neither feels joy nor sorrow.
Regarding "neither obstructed nor submerged":
because one does not give rise to joy upon seeing what is pure and exquisite above,
one likewise feels no sorrow when beholding the foul.
Since one is already free from greed regarding the pure,
one will not now give rise to aversion or obstruction toward the foul;
thus, one does not regard the pure as superior or exalted.
Therefore, one does not give rise to a low rebirth in impure realms.
Rather, one gives rise to joy and reverence in the hearts toward all Buddhas, conceiving the thought that this is something unprecedented.
Although the merits of the Tathāgatas are equal, they manifest different Buddha-lands in order to transform sentient beings.

This clarifies that the paths of all Buddhas are identical and possess no superiority or inferiority; rather, differences are manifested only in accordance with what sentient beings ought to perceive.
"Ānanda, you see the lands of the various Buddhas" and so forth—this citation of a simile serves to clarify the distinction between the true and the responsive bodies.
"The lands are manifold" clarifies that because the buddha-fields are diverse, they possess a specific number;
this serves as a metaphor for the fact that the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) of the Tathāgata possesses distinctions.
"Several" (若干) is a synonym for numerical quantity;
yet space has no "several.
This clarifies that space is utterly vast and transcends all numerical measure, serving as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which is equal and devoid of distinctions such as high or low.
Just as the form-body (rūpakāya) has various [manifestations],
this serves as a metaphor for the fact that the higher stages have various [attainments].
As for that unimpeded wisdom (anāvaraṇaprajñā):
"Uniting with the void" means that the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) and majestic marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of all Buddhas are equal in merit and entirely without distinction; therefore,
from "Samyak" onwards, they are equal in these ten respects.
To briefly cite three of them:
*Samyak-saṃbuddha* means "Perfectly and Fully Awakened One."
"Tathāgata" means "Thus-Come One.
"Buddha" means "Awakened One.
Ānanda, even if I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases in detail, you would not be able to fully grasp them even with a lifespan as long as an eon.
If even the clear and extensive exposition of these three phrases is difficult to fathom, how much more so are his immeasurable merits?
The Bodhisattvas from the upper direction conceived feelings of inferiority toward these three places: the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas in this land, and Vimalakīrti.
Therefore, we now together address Ānanda with urgency regarding the minor matters of the higher realms,
clarifying that all Buddhas are immeasurable.
For this reason, one should not give rise to inferior thoughts.
Let us set aside, Ānanda, what follows and turn instead to the Bodhisattva.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva cannot be fathomed or measured.
While the conditioned and the characterized within the four seas may still be fathomed and measured, [the Bodhisattva is not].
The merit of a bodhisattva is immeasurable.
Ānanda, because you have set aside those below the level of a bodhisattva, I speak again of their abiding in purity.
To clarify the conduct of a bodhisattva from beginning to end, it is fitting that it be difficult to fathom.
The benefit bestowed by Vimalakīrti in a single moment is such that it cannot be fully understood by those of the two vehicles even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Because Vimalakīrti dwells in the body of a layman, they conceive thoughts of inferiority;

now it is clarified that the power of Vimalakīrti’s sudden manifestation of supernatural transformations cannot be exhausted by those of the two vehicles even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
"How inconceivable this is!
At that time, the Bodhisattvas who had come from the World of Universal Fragrance—this concludes the sixth section.
It clarifies that once the Bodhisattvas from the zenith were thus exhorted and urged.
Having attained realization here,
he repented his transgressions, reproached himself, and requested the Dharma before returning to his own land;
this is divided into two questions.
From the beginning until "the Buddha-lands are different" clarifies the confession of transgressions and self-reproach.
From "Thus it is" onwards is the second question.
I request the Dharma so that I may return to my own land.

I pray that you grant me a small portion of the Dharma; having returned to that land, I shall keep the Tathāgata in mind—that is, I shall keep the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s transmission of the mind in mind.
Another interpretation is as follows:
Having already heard the discourse on the inconceivable Buddha-activities,
they were about to request the Dharma and return to their own land.
He desires to proclaim the inconceivable path of the Tathāgata,
so as to cause the sentient beings of his own land to recollect the merits of the Buddha.
This concludes the seventh section, following the Buddha’s address to the bodhisattvas.
This is divided into three sections. The first section,
from "Therein" up to "As for the bodhisattva," states that he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The second pair presents both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the thematic gateways.
Second, from "What is meant by not exhausting the conditioned" down to "his merit is not in vain," this is called the bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned.
This clarifies that one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The third section, from "Furthermore, because they possess merit and virtue" up to "this is called the dharma-gate of liberation through the exhaustive and the inexhaustible," consists of eight phrases that doubly conclude the discussion on the conditioned and the unconditioned; you all should study this.
Regarding the dharma-gate of exhaustion:
what truth is it that, being false and illusory, can be exhausted and extinguished?
This is called "exhaustion."
The true nature of emptiness is indestructible and cannot be extinguished;
this is called "inexhaustible.
Ordinary beings who cling to conditioned phenomena are those who are fully bound.
Those of the two vehicles who cling to emptiness are likewise bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
Because Bodhisattvas dwell within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) without clinging, they are liberated from the fetters of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because they do not realize emptiness [as a final goal] but abide [within it], they are liberated from the fetters of the two vehicles.
Thus, one attains liberation.
That which can serve as a standard is called "Dharma" (the teaching).
Penetrating wisdom constitutes the gateway.
A sūtra passage states:
"The unimpeded" refers to the removal of the obstacles of ordinary beings and the limitations of the two vehicles, and so forth.
What is meant by "exhaustion"? It refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Absence of falsehood is the nature of this Dharma.
What is meant by "exhaustion" and what is meant by "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) dharmas?
That which is empty of intrinsic nature and cannot be exhausted or extinguished is the unconditioned dharma.
As for the Bodhisattva who does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
although the conditioned is false,
if it were exhausted, the great task would not be accomplished.
Although the unconditioned is real,
dwelling upon it causes the contemplation of emptiness to be unclear.
What is meant by not exhausting the conditioned?
The second section explains conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Within this, it is divided into five sub-sections.

The first begins from "not being separated from great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and not abandoning great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)" and extends up to "the cultivation of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) without limit."
To clarify that one’s own practice and external transformation are not separate,
and that one does not depart from great kindness (*maitrī*) nor abandon great compassion (*karuṇā*):
kindness and compassion are the foundation for entering existence and the root for cultivating virtue.
Therefore, this is clarified first.
When Bodhisattvas transform sentient beings, they always take great compassion as their primary principle,
constantly cherishing the bestowing of happiness and the rescuing from suffering.
The mind never abandons it;
one who deeply resolves upon the mind of omniscience and does not neglect or forget it is the embodiment of self-cultivation.
"Clearly looking up to and desiring the fruit of Buddhahood" means that the mind of omniscient wisdom is never forgotten.
"Teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness" clarifies the virtue of outward transformation:
while dwelling within birth and death to transform beings, one’s disposition is free from weariness or indolence.
These two lines clarify that [the Bodhisattva] looks upward toward the fruit of Buddhahood and downward to transform sentient beings.
One who constantly recollects and accords with the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) establishes the primary basis for the aforementioned external transformation of others.
Because he is fully equipped with the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*),
he is able to transform sentient beings without weariness.
Since these four means of integrating beings ensure that there are none who do not comply, it is said that he constantly contemplates and acts in accordance with them.
Those who uphold the True Dharma without sparing their own bodies or lives accomplish the aforementioned self-cultivation and external transformation.

If one praises [the Dharma] yet self-cultivation and external transformation are obstructed and blocked, by protecting the arrival of the Dharma and ensuring its passage, one is able to sacrifice the body and empty the life.
Regarding "planting various roots of goodness without weariness":
this means that because one personally cultivates and extensively plants manifold virtues, which serve as the root for bodhi, one is free from weariness.
Regarding "the mind constantly abiding in skillful means and dedication": [this refers to...]
If one wishes to transform sentient beings, one must employ skillful means without attachment,
dedicating one's own merits toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
This applies to those who seek the Dharma but do not understand it.
This is also one's own practice:
to look up to and entreat the Buddhas for their profound and subtle Dharma,
with a mind free from indolence or stinginess.
Regarding "not being stingy in preaching the Dharma":
this practice of outward transformation arises precisely from one's own ability to seek the Dharma.
To transform sentient beings with what one has attained oneself, without any stinginess;
to diligently make offerings to all Buddhas is the primary cause for seeking the Dharma above.
Diligently making offerings to all Buddhas and being able to seek the Dharma without weariness—
therefore, one enters into birth and death without fear;
this is precisely because of the aforementioned practice of teaching the Dharma without stinginess.
Because they are fearless regarding birth and death, they are able to preach the Dharma without stinginess.
Regarding all honors and insults, their minds are free from sorrow or joy;
whereas ordinary people have their minds disturbed by receiving honor or insult.
The Bodhisattva remains detached from the eight worldly dharmas, giving rise to neither sorrow nor joy therein.
He does not disparage those who have recently begun their studies, but honors those who study as he would the Buddha;
for by studying, one will surely attain realization, and thus they must not be disparaged.
Those who have already trained will certainly attain Buddhahood;
they should be revered as Buddhas.
They cause those fallen into afflictions to give rise to right mindfulness.
Since it is fundamentally never emerged,
why is it called "falling"?
It is merely that through the practice of subduing afflictions, one gives rise to the intention of renunciation.
Only when one encounters conditions and regresses from practice is one said to have fallen; at such a time,
it is appropriate to teach and transform them,
causing them to give rise to right mindfulness so that they do not regard the bliss of seclusion as a source of burning affliction.
The bodies of those of the two vehicles are far removed from clamor and their minds are free from afflictions, abiding in peace through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although the bodies of Bodhisattvas are likewise far removed from clamor and their minds are free from afflictions, [they differ in that they do not abide in the unconditioned].
Even if one uses the path as a mere means, one does not regard it as precious.
One who does not cling to their own happiness but rejoices in the happiness of others is unlike the ordinary person,
who gives rise to jealousy when seeing others obtain happiness.
When one obtains pleasure for oneself, the emotions become attached;
seeing others suffer, the mind remains at ease;
but when one suffers oneself, the emotions are stirred.
The bodhisattva is not like this;
he does not dwell on his own pleasure,
but when he hears of the pleasure of others, his heart gives rise to joy and gladness.
Regarding those who conceive of the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as being like hell:
although these concentrations are pleasant and peaceful, if one remains attached to them, the Great Way will not be accomplished.
One should have no emotional attachment to them, regarding them as if they were hell.
Regarding those who contemplate saṃsāra as being like a garden:
although saṃsāra is suffering, the cause of the Great Path arises from it.
Bodhisattvas delight in wandering within it, just as one contemplates a garden.
Regarding those who come seeking [something] as being like a virtuous teacher:
when one sees someone coming to beg from me,
one conceives of them as a virtuous teacher.
With a joyful heart,
they employ skillful means to exhort and transform others, leading them to enter the True Dharma.
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:

When seeing someone come to seek wealth or request the Dharma, one should conceive of them as a "good teacher. This is because the teacher’s fundamental purpose is to benefit me; when a person comes and achieves success through my influence, the merit returns to me.
Since this is the very meaning of being benefited, one should conceive of them as a good teacher.
One who relinquishes all possessions while maintaining the perception of omniscience knows that this giving is endowed with omniscience;
clearly seeing cause and effect, they give without regret.
To conceive the thought of providing protection upon seeing those who violate the precepts;
to conceive the thought of skillfully rescuing and receiving those who commit evil and defile the Brahma-conduct;
and to regard the various pāramitās as one's parents.
This is intended to clarify that the various perfections (pāramitās) of a bodhisattva are able to generate and sustain the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), just as parents do for a child.
Furthermore,
it is explained that when a child has needs, they rely upon their parents for support.
This clarifies that what a bodhisattva requires is sought within the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Regarding the thought of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) as one's retinue:
it is because these factors of enlightenment cause me to be honored and preeminent.
Just as worldly people have kinsmen who increase their own dignity,
so too does one who cultivates roots of goodness without limit; yet,
this superior confusion of clarity obstructs both one's own practice and external transformation.
This is the summary:
one is able to practice all wholesome dharmas.
This is the second section.
From the description of the adornments of the various pure lands down to the hearing of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues, [the text] demonstrates that one should remain resolute without withdrawing.
It clearly sets forth the fruit of Buddhahood to manifest three kinds of excellence, thereby establishing and bringing forth his practice.
Since the preceding section has clarified that through one's own practice and external transformation one will necessarily attain the fruit of Buddhahood,
it next cites three matters regarding the fruit of Buddhahood to establish and manifest those practices.
This is done by means of the adornments of various pure lands, which constitute the perfection of a Buddha-field.
This is the first matter.
It clarifies that because one seeks to adorn the pure land of the Buddha-fruit, one practices and abides in the essentials to accomplish one's own buddha-field.
As for "opening the gates and practicing great giving to fulfill the marks and signs":
This is the second matter.
Giving can fundamentally support the administration of justice;
therefore, by practicing giving within the causal stage, one can fully realize the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Buddha’s fruition.
There may be a mind inclined toward giving while material wealth is scarce, or a mind inclined toward giving while material wealth is abundant;
in these two cases, one is incomplete and cannot respond to requests from all quarters.
When these two are both fully provided so that one may have whatever is required—
those who eliminate all evils, purify body, speech, and mind, and possess the courage to endure throughout countless kalpas of birth and death—
they accomplish the second superior matter.
When the cause is pure, the fruit is sublime.
This is precisely because one can eliminate all evils and purify the three types of equality;
by fearlessly transforming sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death, one attains the Dharma-body of the Pure Land.
To hear of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues and to remain resolute without weariness—
this is the third matter.
It clarifies that upon hearing of the Buddha’s immeasurable merits, one practices, abides, and maintains one's vows without indolence.
Third, from "by means of the sword of wisdom" down to "with great vigor he crushes the armies of Māra," it clarifies that there is something to be eliminated.
Having already distinguished the fruit above, these [passages] manifest three kinds of superior matters.
Unless one eliminates the two burdens of cause and effect,
there is no way to attain [the goal];
therefore, this is explained next.
To destroy the thieves of affliction with the sword of wisdom is itself a causal burden;
for afflictions are able to plunder the virtuous wealth of persons.
It is like a thief;
because the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness can destroy afflictions, it is said to be like a sword.
As for "exiting the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases":
To eliminate the two māras of the aggregates and death is itself the burden of fruition;
to shoulder the responsibility for sentient beings so that they may attain eternal liberation is [the bodhisattva's vow].
Having already exerted oneself to free oneself from these burdens,
one is further able to shoulder the burden of sentient beings,
ensuring their eternal liberation from the two burdens of cause and effect.
Regarding "subduing the armies of Māra through great diligence":
because the celestial Māras are the conditions that give rise to evil,
one is able to conquer them through the practice of diligence.
The fourth section, from "constantly seeking non-conceptuality" onwards, concludes with the cultivation of the four immeasurables and clarifies the two practices of emptiness and existence.
Having already clarified that which is to be eliminated above, [the following now addresses] that which is to be cultivated.
Were it not for contemplating the object of emptiness as its opposite,
one would be unable to eliminate the three māras— of afflictions, aggregates, and death.
This is possible only if there is sufficient wisdom.
How can one subdue the celestial Māras?
Therefore, this is explained next:
"One who constantly seeks the wisdom of the true mark of non-conceptualization."
Maintaining the boundary is the mindfulness;
because the principle of emptiness is devoid of objects and should be held in the mind, it is called "non-mindfulness.
The principle of emptiness transcends all that is provisional and deceptive, and is thus the reality.
It is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it manifests as distinct from existence.
Regarding "wisdom": this refers to the practice of these various contemplative wisdoms.
The passage beginning with "having few desires and being content, yet not abandoning the world" clarifies the wisdom regarding existence (*bhava*).
Were it not for his possession of the complete wisdom of the Middle Way,
he would have been unable to subdue the celestial Māras;
yet while his inner mind constantly practiced the dharma of few desires and contentment, he outwardly manifested the ways of those in the world with many desires.
Furthermore,
it is explained that while the practice of the śrāvaka consists of having few desires and knowing contentment to abandon the world and enter nirvāṇa,
the practice of the bodhisattva consists of having few desires and knowing contentment without abandoning the world to enter nirvāṇa.
Those who can follow along without violating their dignified demeanor;
those who can conform to worldly customs without violating the dignified demeanor of the True Dharma;
and those who manifest various types of dignified demeanor to give rise to supernatural powers and wisdom for the purpose of guiding sentient beings onto the Path.
He constantly uses the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to transform and guide sentient beings.
These five supernormal powers are the fruits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Through concentration, one attains the dhāraṇīs.
One who attains the dhāraṇī of mindfulness such that what has been heard is never forgotten,
attains the dhāraṇī of retention; thus,
there shall be no loss regarding the characteristics of sounds and phenomena.
Having skillfully distinguished the various faculties and severed the doubts of sentient beings, he now proceeds to the main body of the text.
Internally upholding *dhāraṇī* and externally possessing eloquence (*pratibhāna*), he preaches the Dharma for the sake of beings.
However, in order to preach the Dharma, one must first know the faculties in order to understand the appropriate medicine.

Therefore, first clarifying the faculties of consciousness and knowing the medicines to sever the doubts of sentient beings through their various faculties is what clarifies the recognition of the illness.
If one knows the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings, one can skillfully bestow the Dharma according to their capacities to sever their doubts.
Alternatively, one may expound the Dharma with unhindered eloquence through the power of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
It is precisely because one has attained such unimpeded eloquence that one is able to sever the doubts of sentient beings.

Those who purify the ten paths of wholesome action and receive the blessings of humans and devas do so precisely because of their practice of the ten wholesome deeds; thus they are able to manifest among humans and devas to receive blessings and provide instruction.
Those who cultivate the four immeasurables and open the path to the Brahma heavens do so likewise.
Because they internally cultivate the practice of the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), they are able to manifest birth in the four dhyānas.
The four dhyānas refer to the four Brahmā heavens.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas who are of one essence seek birth in the Brahmā heavens because they desire to act as lords of all dharmas.

The fifth section, from the exhortation to preach the Dharma down to the end of the "Chapter on Not Losing Wholesome Dharmas," clarifies the purity of the three karmas as the conclusion of the preceding four sections. This is because,
by virtue of the purity of body, speech, and mind, one is fully equipped with the dharmas of the aforementioned four sections.
Regarding "exhorting [the Buddha] to preach the Dharma, rejoicing in it, and praising it well, one obtains the voice of a Buddha":
this clarifies that because the vocal karma is pure, one obtains the subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice of a Buddha.
Regarding "through goodness of body, speech, and mind, one obtains the majestic deportment of a Buddha": [this clarifies that through such purity, one attains the physical presence of a Buddha].

By clarifying the purity of bodily karma, one attains the elephant-king gaze of a Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, every movement and deportment is in perfect accord with the body cultivated for the Path, such that speech and mind follow one another in harmony.
